canonical_question: How does the observed coarsening of oxide particles at 1400 °C specifically affect the crack initiation sites compared to the splintery morphology at lower temperatures?

question_variants.question: How does the observed coarsening of oxide particles at 1400 °C specifically affect the crack initiation sites compared to the splintery morphology at lower temperatures?
question_variants.resolution_summary: The text confirms that oxide particles change from splintery (polyangular) to circular at 1400 °C and notes that coarse inclusions can serve as crack initiation sources. However, it does not explicitly compare the crack initiation risk of the circular morphology versus the splintery morphology.

answers.answer: The paper states that at 1400 °C, oxide particles became circular instead of splintery (polyangular). It also identifies coarse inclusions of oxides at this temperature as sources of crack initiation in the BCC-matrix. While it links coarse particles to crack initiation, it does not explicitly contrast the specific risk of circular morphology against splintery morphology.
answers.measurement_outcome: Particle shape change: splintery to circular; coarse inclusions act as crack sources
answers.mechanism: Coarse inclusions serve as sources of crack initiation
answers.boundary_limitation: No explicit comparison of crack initiation susceptibility between circular and splintery morphologies.
evidence_spans: Their volume fraction decreases when the SPS temperature increases and accounts for 21.5 vol.% at 1300 °C and 11.5 vol.% at 1400 °C.
The coarse inclusions can serve as sources of crack initiation in the BCC-matrix.
